n: Passover and the week-long Feast of Unleavened Bread were two days away. The chief priests and scribes were looking for a sneaky way to arrest and kill Jesus.

f.g: The yearly feast remembering Israel’s deliverance from Egypt, when the destroying angel “passed over” homes marked with lamb’s blood.

n: They wanted to avoid the feast itself, when Jerusalem was packed with pilgrims who might riot in Jesus’ defense.

At a dinner in Bethany at the home of Simon the leper (probably someone Jesus had healed), a woman broke open an alabaster jar of very costly perfume and poured it on Jesus’ head. John identifies her as Mary, sister of Martha.

f.g: A sealed flask of soft translucent stone; breaking its neck meant using it all.
Nard, a fragrant oil from a plant grown in the Himalayas — extremely expensive.

n: Some at the table were indignant: why waste such ointment?
It could have sold for over three hundred denarii — about a year’s wages — and the money given to the poor. They scolded her harshly.

f.g: 300 denarii, nearly a laborer’s yearly income.

n: Jesus defended her: leave her alone. She has done a beautiful thing for me.
There will always be poor people to help, and you should help them; but Jesus would not be with them much longer.

f.w: ye have the poor with you always

n: She did what she could, anointing his body ahead of time for burial. Whether she fully understood or not, her act honored his coming death.

f.w: She hath done what she could

n: Jesus promised that wherever the gospel is preached, her act of devotion would be told in her memory — and it still is.
In stark contrast, Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, went to the chief priests to betray Jesus.
They were delighted and promised him money. Matthew says it was thirty pieces of silver. Judas began watching for a good opportunity.
On the first day of Unleavened Bread, when Passover lambs were sacrificed at the temple, the disciples asked where to prepare the Passover meal.

f.g: Lambs were slaughtered at the temple on the afternoon of the 14th of Nisan.

n: Jesus sent two disciples into the city to follow a man carrying a water jar — unusual, since women normally carried water, so he would be easy to spot.
They were to ask the homeowner where the Teacher’s guest room was for the Passover. Jesus had likely arranged this quietly to keep the location secret from Judas.

f.g: Master or owner of the house.

n: He would show them a large upstairs room, already furnished. There they should prepare.

f.g: An upstairs room, often used for guests and gatherings.

n: Everything happened just as Jesus said, and they prepared the Passover.
That evening Jesus arrived with the Twelve.
While they reclined and ate, Jesus said one of them, someone eating with him, would betray him. Betrayal by a table companion was especially painful.

f.w: One of you which eateth with me

n: Grieved, they asked one by one, “Is it I?” Each was willing to examine himself.

f.g: The Greek expects the answer “no” — “Surely not I?”

n: Jesus said it was one of the Twelve, someone dipping bread in the same bowl with him.

f.w: dippeth with me in the dish
f.g: Bread was dipped in a shared bowl of sauce at the Passover meal.

n: The Son of Man would go to his death as scripture foretold, but terrible sorrow awaits his betrayer — better for him never to have been born.

f.w: as it is written of him

n: During the meal Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to them: “Take, eat: this is my body.” He instituted the sacrament, a lasting reminder of his sacrifice.

f.g: The JST adds “in remembrance of my body,” showing it is a symbol.

n: He took the cup, gave thanks, and passed it to them, and they all drank.
“This is my blood of the new covenant, shed for many.” As blood sealed the old covenant at Sinai, Christ’s blood seals a new covenant.
Jesus would not drink wine again until he drinks it new in God’s kingdom. Latter-day Saint scripture says he will partake of the sacrament again with his disciples at his coming.

f.w: drink it new in the kingdom of God

n: After singing a hymn — likely the Hallel psalms traditionally sung at Passover — they went out to the Mount of Olives.

f.g: Probably from Psalms 113-118, sung at the Passover meal.

n: Jesus warned that they would all stumble and fall away that night, fulfilling Zechariah: strike the shepherd and the sheep scatter.
But a promise of hope: after he rose, he would go ahead of them to Galilee.

f.w: I will go before you into Galilee

n: Peter insisted that even if everyone else fell away, he never would.
Jesus told him that this very night, before the rooster crowed twice, Peter would deny him three times. Only Mark mentions “twice.”
Peter protested even more strongly: even if I must die with you, I will never deny you. All the others said the same.
They came to Gethsemane, a garden on the Mount of Olives. Jesus told the disciples to sit while he prayed.

f.g: Aramaic “oil press” — an olive grove where olives were crushed for oil.

n: He took Peter, James, and John further and began to be deeply distressed and troubled — overwhelmed, as Mark’s strong words show.

f.g: Deeply alarmed, overwhelmed with awe and distress.

n: He told them his soul was crushed with sorrow to the point of death and asked them to stay and keep watch.
Going a little farther, he fell to the ground and prayed that, if possible, this hour might pass from him. Here in Gethsemane the Savior began to take upon himself the sins and suffering of all.
“Abba, Father” — an intimate, trusting address. All things are possible for you; take this cup from me. Yet not my will, but yours. This is the heart of perfect submission.

f.g: Aramaic for “Father,” a warm, family word used by children and adults.

f.w: not what I will, but what thou wilt

n: He came back and found them asleep. He asked Peter — calling him Simon, his old name — couldn’t you stay awake even one hour?
Stay awake and pray so you won’t fall into temptation. The spirit is willing, but the body is weak. A tender acknowledgment of human limits.
He went away again and prayed the same words.
Returning, he found them asleep again; their eyes were heavy, and they didn’t know what to say to him.
The third time he said, “Enough — the hour has come.” The Son of Man was being handed over to sinners.
“Get up, let’s go. My betrayer is here.” Jesus went out to meet what was coming.
Immediately Judas arrived with an armed crowd sent by the chief priests, scribes, and elders, carrying swords and clubs.
Judas had arranged a signal: the man I kiss is the one — arrest him and take him away under guard.
He went straight to Jesus, said “Rabbi,” and kissed him warmly. A sign of love became the tool of betrayal.

f.g: A common greeting between a disciple and his teacher; Mark’s word suggests an affectionate kiss.

n: They seized Jesus and arrested him.
One bystander (John says it was Peter) drew a sword and cut off the ear of the high priest’s servant. Luke records that Jesus healed it.
Jesus asked why they came with weapons as if he were a violent bandit.
He had taught openly in the temple every day, and they never arrested him. But this was happening to fulfill the scriptures.
All the disciples abandoned him and ran away, just as he had foretold.
A young man wearing only a linen sheet was following, and the soldiers grabbed him. Many think this detail, found only in Mark, refers to Mark himself.

f.g: A sheet or light garment of linen.

n: He slipped out of the sheet and ran away naked. Even the last follower fled.
They took Jesus to the high priest, Caiaphas, where the chief priests, elders, and scribes — the ruling council — had gathered.

f.g: Caiaphas, high priest from about AD 18 to 36.

n: Peter followed at a distance into the high priest’s courtyard and sat with the guards warming himself by the fire. He was brave enough to follow, but from afar.

f.g: Here the courtyard of the high priest’s residence.

n: The council looked for testimony to justify a death sentence but couldn’t find any.

f.g: The Sanhedrin, the 71-member Jewish high court.

n: Many gave false testimony, but their stories didn’t match. The law required two witnesses who agreed.
Some stood up and testified falsely against him…
…claiming he said he would destroy this man-made temple and build another in three days without hands. They twisted his words about his own body.
Even then their testimony didn’t agree.
The high priest stood and demanded: aren’t you going to answer these charges?
Jesus stayed silent, like the lamb in Isaiah. Then the high priest asked directly: are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One? (“Blessed” was a reverent way to avoid saying God’s name.)
Jesus answered plainly: “I am.” And they would see the Son of Man seated at God’s right hand and coming with the clouds — combining Psalm 110 and Daniel 7.

f.w: sitting on the right hand of power

n: The high priest tore his robes — a dramatic sign of grief or outrage at blasphemy — and said no more witnesses were needed.

f.g: Tore his garments — a ritual reaction to hearing blasphemy.

n: “You have heard the blasphemy. What is your verdict?” They all condemned him as deserving death.
Some spat on him, blindfolded him, struck him, and mocked: “Prophesy!” — tell us who hit you. The guards beat him too. Ironically, his prophecies were being fulfilled at that very moment.
Meanwhile, below in the courtyard, one of the high priest’s servant girls came by.
Seeing Peter by the fire, she stared and said, “You were with Jesus of Nazareth too.”
Peter denied it, pretending not to understand, and moved out to the gateway. A rooster crowed.
The servant girl saw him again and told the bystanders, “He’s one of them.”
Peter denied it again. Soon the bystanders pressed him: surely you’re one of them — your Galilean accent gives you away.

f.g: Your accent matches — Galileans had a recognizable way of speaking.

n: Peter began to call down curses on himself and swear oaths: “I don’t know this man you’re talking about.” He wouldn’t even say Jesus’ name.

f.g: To invoke curses on himself if he was lying and to take oaths — not simply crude language.

n: Immediately the rooster crowed a second time. Peter remembered Jesus’ words and broke down weeping. His bitter tears began the repentance that would make him a mighty apostle.
